messages.content: What's the composition of species in my backyard garden in Boston?

function.name: soil_composition_analyze
function.description: Analyzes the composition of the soil including percentage of sand, silt, and clay based on the given soil sample. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

location.description: The location where the soil sample is collected from.

soil_sample.description: The binary representation of the soil sample.

season.description: The season during which the soil sample is collected.

message.content:
I don’t actually have access to your backyard’s plants, so I can’t give you a precise inventory right now. However, here’s what you can do next: | Step | What to Do | Why It Helps | |------|------------|--------------| | **1️⃣ Take Photos** | Snap clear pictures of each distinct shrub, tree, flower bed, lawn area, and even weeds. Try different angles (top‑down, side view). | Visual records make it easier for experts—or AI image classifiers—to recognize species. | | **2️⃣ Use Plant ID Apps** | Upload those images into free identification tools such as *iNaturalist*, *PlantSnap*, *PictureThis*, or *Google Lens*. | These services compare your photo against millions of labeled specimens and often return a ranked list of possible matches along with confidence scores. | | **3️⃣ Record Observations Manually** | Write down obvious traits—leaf shape, bark texture, fruit type, flowering time—and note the exact spot (e.g., “northwest corner near the fence”). | Detailed notes help narrow down candidates when automated methods produce multiple possibilities. | | **4️⃣ Consult Local Resources** | Check out resources specific to New England/Boston flora:
• Massachusetts Horticultural Society
• Harvard University Extension Garden Guides
• State Natural Heritage Program lists | Regional guides filter out exotic species unlikely to grow there and highlight native ones common to Boston lawns. | | **5️⃣ Ask a Professional** | If you’re still unsure, bring samples or photos to a local nursery, university botany department, or community gardening group. | Human botanists can confirm tricky identifications and advise on care or removal if needed. | ### Quick Reference List – Common Species Found in Boston Backyards | Category | Typical Examples | Notes | |----------|------------------|-------| | **Trees & Shrubs** | Red Maple (*Acer rubrum*), Eastern White Pine (*Pinus strobus*), Boxwood (*Buxus sempervirens*) | Many are ornamental but also serve as windbreaks. | | **Perennials / Groundcovers** | Hostas, Daylilies, Creeping Thyme | Often used under trees or in shaded beds. | | **Annual Flowers** | Marigolds, Petunias, Zinnias | Seasonal color boosters. | | **Lawns** | Kentucky Bluegrass, Perennial Ryegrass | Standard turf grasses in the region. | | **Common Invasive/Weedy Plants** | Japanese Knotweed, Garlic Mustard, English Ivy | Watch for these—they can dominate quickly. | --- #### Next Steps If you’d like me to walk through interpreting results from one of those apps or help set up a simple spreadsheet to track your findings, just let me know!
